notes.meaning: God calls Moses, Aaron, his two oldest sons, and seventy elders to climb part of the mountain. These leaders were chosen to represent all the tribes of Israel as witnesses of God's presence. Even though they were honored leaders, they still had to bow and worship from a distance before the holy God.

Only Moses is permitted to draw near to the Lord on the mountain peak, while the other leaders and the rest of the people must stay back. Moses served as a mediator, a go-between who represented the people to God and brought God's word back to them. In this unique role, Moses pointed ahead to Jesus, who alone enters God's holy presence on our behalf.

Moses comes down from the mountain and recites all the laws and commands God had given him. The people answer together with one voice, promising to obey everything the Lord has said. God did not force the people into this agreement blindly, but gave them the chance to hear and accept the terms freely.

Moses writes down all of God's words so that Israel would have a permanent, written record. Early the next morning, he builds an altar at the foot of Mount Sinai and sets up twelve stone pillars. The altar represented God, and the twelve pillars represented the twelve tribes of Israel entering into this sacred agreement.

Moses sends young men to offer animal sacrifices on the altar, including burnt offerings and peace offerings. These young men were selected for their strength and energy to handle and sacrifice the heavy oxen. In these sacrifices, animal lives were given to show devotion to God and to prepare the way for peace between him and his people.

Moses divides the blood from the sacrifices into two portions, putting half into large basins and splashing the other half against the altar. Splashing blood on the altar showed that the people dedicated their lives to God and that God accepted their offering. Dividing the blood prepared the way to bind both God and the people together in one solemn covenant.

Moses takes the Book of the Covenant, which contained the written laws, and reads it aloud to the assembled nation. The people confirm their commitment by promising again to listen, obey, and do all that the Lord has commanded. Hearing the words read aloud ensured that everyone knew the holy standard they were pledging to follow.

Moses takes the blood from the basins and sprinkles it over the people, declaring it to be the blood of the covenant. A covenant is a sacred, binding promise between God and his people. The sprinkling showed that Israel was cleansed and brought into fellowship with God through sacrifice, pointing ahead to how Jesus shed his blood to seal the new covenant.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Church teaches that when Jesus called the cup the 'blood of the covenant' at the Last Supper, he made the Eucharist the true ratifying sacrifice of the New Covenant, meaning the wine substantially becomes his literal blood.

notes.meaning: Moses leads Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders up the mountain as God had directed. Now that the covenant blood had been sprinkled, these chosen men could safely step onto the holy mountain on behalf of the nation. Their climb placed trustworthy witnesses in position to see God's glory and verify his truth to Israel.

The elders are given a glimpse of the God of Israel in heavenly splendor. Under his feet they see a dazzling pavement that looks like clear sapphire, glowing as bright and pure as the open sky. God did not reveal an earthly body that could be copied into an idol, but let them behold the majestic foundation of his heavenly throne.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars, noting the ancient Greek translation, understand the text to mean the elders saw only the place where God stood or caught sight of the floor while prostrate, since Scripture elsewhere teaches God has no visible form.

notes.meaning: God shows great mercy by not striking down the leaders of Israel, even though people rightly feared they could not see God and live. Instead, the elders look upon God's glory and eat and drink together in peace. Sharing this sacrificial meal on the mountain proved that God had accepted them and welcomed them into warm fellowship.

The Lord calls Moses to go higher up the mountain and wait there to receive stone tablets. God himself had written the law and commandments on these tablets so the people could be taught and always remember them. Moses was willing to remain on the mountain as long as God required in order to receive his commands.

Moses sets out with his assistant Joshua to climb further up the mountain of God. Joshua was being trained to become Israel's future leader by learning how to seek the Lord and draw near to him. He served as Moses' trusted companion during the initial climb before Moses went on into the thick cloud.

Moses tells the elders to remain where they are until he returns, leaving Aaron and Hur in charge of settling legal disputes. A faithful leader makes sure the people are cared for even while he is away so that peace and justice continue in the camp. This instruction left Israel with clear guidance on where to turn for help during his absence.

As Moses climbs higher onto the mountain, a thick cloud wraps around the peak. The cloud was a visible sign of God's special presence, assuring Moses that God was there while keeping his full majesty hidden from human eyes. Moses paused at the edge of the cloud in quiet reverence, waiting for God's call.

The glory of the Lord settles upon Mount Sinai, and the cloud covers the mountain for six full days. On the seventh day, God calls out to Moses from the midst of the cloud. This period of patient waiting prepared Moses' heart in quiet contemplation before stepping into the immediate presence of God.

To the people watching from the camp below, God's glory looked like a blazing, devouring fire on top of the mountain. This fearsome sight displayed God's intense holiness and absolute power to the whole nation. It taught Israel to treat God's law with the deepest reverence and godly fear.

Moses boldly enters the cloud and climbs to the top of the mountain, where he stays for forty days and forty nights. God miraculously sustained his life during this entire time without any food or water. Moses spent this extended season listening to God's voice and receiving the plans for God's dwelling place among his people.
